concepts.name: Intermolecular and intramolecular forces
concepts.statement: Intramolecular forces are the bonds within a molecule that keep it together; intermolecular forces are the attractions between molecules, and they decide many of a substance’s physical properties. The intermolecular forces between small molecules are usually weak compared to the bonds within them.

concepts.name: The phase of a substance depends on its intermolecular forces and kinetic energy
concepts.statement: Intermolecular forces hold particles close together, whereas the particles’ kinetic energy works to separate them, so the phase of a substance depends on the balance between the two. Cooling a gas or compressing it lets the attractions win and it condenses; cooling a liquid far enough lets it freeze.

concepts.name: London dispersion forces
concepts.statement: Because the electrons of an atom or molecule are in constant motion, it can develop an instantaneous dipole, which in turn induces a dipole in a neighbor; the two temporary dipoles attract. This dispersion force is present in all condensed phases, whatever the atoms or molecules.

concepts.name: Larger, more polarizable particles have stronger dispersion forces
concepts.statement: In a larger atom the valence electrons are farther from the nucleus and less tightly held, so the electron cloud is more easily distorted; a more polarizable particle has larger dispersion forces and a higher melting and boiling point.

concepts.name: Molecular shape and contact area affect dispersion forces
concepts.statement: Molecules with the same formula can have different dispersion forces: an elongated molecule offers more surface area for contact with its neighbors than a compact one, and so it is held more strongly.

concepts.name: Dipole-dipole attractions
concepts.statement: A polar molecule has a partial positive end and a partial negative end, and the positive end of one polar molecule attracts the negative end of another. These attractions add to the dispersion forces, so a polar substance boils higher than a nonpolar one of similar mass.

concepts.name: Hydrogen bonding
concepts.statement: When hydrogen is bonded to fluorine, oxygen or nitrogen, the large difference in electronegativity and the small sizes of the atoms concentrate the partial charges, and the attraction to a similar group in a nearby molecule is a particularly strong dipole-dipole attraction called a hydrogen bond. It is much weaker than a covalent bond but stronger than other intermolecular attractions.

concepts.name: Identifying the intermolecular forces in a substance and ranking boiling points
concepts.statement: To compare substances, we identify the forces each can have from its structure: dispersion forces always, dipole-dipole attractions if the molecule is polar, and hydrogen bonding if it has an H–F, H–O or H–N group. With similar sizes, the substance with the stronger forces has the higher boiling point; with the same kind of force, the larger molecule does.

concepts.name: Intermolecular force
concepts.statement: An intermolecular force is a noncovalent attractive force between atoms, molecules or ions. Intermolecular forces are much weaker than the bonds within molecules, yet they decide many physical properties.

concepts.name: Van der Waals force
concepts.statement: A van der Waals force is an attractive or repulsive force between molecules, a name that covers dipole-dipole attractions, dipole-induced dipole attractions and London dispersion forces.

concepts.name: Instantaneous dipole
concepts.statement: An instantaneous dipole is a temporary dipole that exists for a brief moment when the electrons of an atom or molecule happen to be distributed unevenly.

concepts.name: Induced dipole
concepts.statement: An induced dipole is a temporary dipole formed when the electrons of an atom or molecule are distorted by the instantaneous dipole of a neighboring atom or molecule.

concepts.name: Polarizability
concepts.statement: Polarizability is a measure of how easily a charge can distort the electron cloud of an atom or molecule. Larger atoms and molecules, whose valence electrons are held less tightly, are more polarizable.

concepts.name: Viscosity
concepts.statement: The viscosity of a liquid is its resistance to flow. It is greater for liquids of structurally complex molecules with strong intermolecular forces, and it decreases as the temperature rises and the molecules move more rapidly.

concepts.name: Cohesive and adhesive forces
concepts.statement: Cohesive forces are the attractions between identical molecules of a liquid; adhesive forces are the attractions between the liquid and different molecules, such as those of a surface. Their relative strength decides whether a liquid wets a surface and which way its meniscus curves.

concepts.name: Surface tension
concepts.statement: Molecules at the surface of a liquid are attracted by only about half as many neighbors as molecules within it, so the liquid contracts to the smallest surface. Surface tension is the energy required to increase the surface area of a liquid; it makes a small drop spherical and lets a water strider stand on water.

concepts.name: Capillary action
concepts.statement: When the adhesive forces between a liquid and a narrow tube or porous material are strong, combined with the cohesive forces within the liquid, the liquid flows upward against gravity until its weight balances the attraction. The narrower the tube, the higher the liquid climbs.

concepts.name: The height of capillary rise, $h = 2T\cos\theta / r\rho g$
concepts.statement: The height to which a liquid rises in a capillary tube is directly proportional to its surface tension and to the cosine of the contact angle, and inversely proportional to the radius of the tube and the density of the liquid. For water in glass the contact angle is 0°.

forms.condition: a liquid in a capillary tube of radius r

concepts.name: Cohesive force
concepts.statement: A cohesive force is a force of attraction between identical molecules, such as the molecules of a liquid.

concepts.name: Adhesive force
concepts.statement: An adhesive force is a force of attraction between molecules of different chemical identities, such as a liquid and the surface it touches.

concepts.name: Vapor pressure and dynamic equilibrium
concepts.statement: In a closed container, a liquid vaporizes until the rate of condensation equals the rate of vaporization; the amounts of liquid and vapor then stop changing, though molecules continue to be exchanged. The pressure of the vapor in this dynamic equilibrium is the liquid’s vapor pressure, and it does not depend on the surface area or the size of the vessel.

concepts.name: Stronger intermolecular forces mean a lower vapor pressure
concepts.statement: Strong intermolecular attractions impede vaporization and favor the recapture of gas molecules, so a liquid with stronger forces has a lower vapor pressure.

concepts.name: Vapor pressure rises with temperature
concepts.statement: At a higher temperature a greater fraction of the molecules have enough kinetic energy to escape the liquid, and those that escape move faster, so the vapor pressure increases.

concepts.name: Boiling point and normal boiling point
concepts.statement: A liquid boils when its vapor pressure equals the pressure of the gas above it, so its boiling point depends on the surrounding pressure; the normal boiling point is the boiling point at 1 atm (101.3 kPa). A vapor pressure curve can be read as the boiling point at each pressure.

concepts.name: The Clausius-Clapeyron equation
concepts.statement: The vapor pressure of a liquid depends exponentially on temperature, $P = Ae^{-\Delta H_{\text{vap}}/RT}$, so a plot of ln P against 1/T is a straight line whose slope is −ΔH<sub>vap</sub>/R. Temperature must be in kelvin.

forms.condition: the vapor pressure of a liquid, with T in kelvin

concepts.name: Using the two-point Clausius-Clapeyron equation
concepts.statement: Given the vapor pressure at two temperatures, we can solve the two-point form for the enthalpy of vaporization; given one pair and the enthalpy of vaporization, we can find the vapor pressure at another temperature or the boiling point at another pressure.

forms.condition: two vapor pressure-temperature pairs of one liquid

concepts.name: Enthalpies of vaporization, fusion, and sublimation
concepts.statement: Melting, vaporization and sublimation are endothermic, and freezing, condensation and deposition release the same heat with the opposite sign. Melting only partly overcomes the intermolecular attractions while vaporization overcomes them completely, so ΔH<sub>fus</sub> is less than ΔH<sub>vap</sub>, and by Hess’s law ΔH<sub>sub</sub> is about their sum.

forms.condition: sublimation modeled as melting followed by vaporization (Hess's law)

concepts.name: Heating and cooling curves
concepts.statement: As a substance is heated at a steady rate, its temperature rises within each phase, as q = mcΔT describes, and stays constant at each phase transition while the heat goes into overcoming intermolecular attractions. The plateaus of a heating curve are its phase transitions.

concepts.name: Calculating the total heat to change temperature and phase
concepts.statement: The heat for a change through several phases is the sum of the steps: q = mcΔT for each warming or cooling within a phase, with the specific heat of that phase, and q = nΔH for each transition.

concepts.name: Vaporization
concepts.statement: Vaporization is the change from the liquid state to the gaseous state.

concepts.name: Condensation
concepts.statement: Condensation is the change from the gaseous state to the liquid state.

concepts.name: Melting
concepts.statement: Melting is the change from the solid state to the liquid state.

concepts.name: Freezing
concepts.statement: Freezing is the change from the liquid state to the solid state.

concepts.name: Sublimation
concepts.statement: Sublimation is the change from the solid state directly to the gaseous state.

concepts.name: Deposition
concepts.statement: Deposition is the change from the gaseous state directly to the solid state.

concepts.name: Dynamic equilibrium
concepts.statement: A dynamic equilibrium is the state of a system in which reciprocal processes occur at equal rates, so that nothing changes overall although both processes continue.

concepts.name: Vapor pressure, $P$
concepts.statement: The vapor pressure, or equilibrium vapor pressure, of a liquid or solid is the pressure exerted by its vapor in equilibrium with it at a given temperature.

concepts.name: Normal boiling point
concepts.statement: The normal boiling point of a liquid is the temperature at which its vapor pressure equals 1 atm (760 torr).

concepts.name: Melting point and freezing point
concepts.statement: The melting point of a substance is the temperature at which its solid and liquid phases are in equilibrium. The same temperature is called the freezing point when it is reached by cooling the liquid.

concepts.name: Phase diagrams
concepts.statement: A phase diagram combines the pressure-temperature curves of the liquid-gas, solid-liquid and solid-gas equilibria of a substance. Each region is the phase that is stable under those conditions, and each curve gives a transition temperature as a function of pressure.

concepts.name: Reading states and phase changes from a phase diagram
concepts.statement: To find the state of a substance, we locate the temperature and pressure on its phase diagram and read the region; to find the phase changes on heating at constant pressure, or on compression at constant temperature, we follow a horizontal or vertical line and note the curves it crosses.

concepts.name: The triple point
concepts.statement: The triple point is the temperature and pressure at which the solid, liquid and gas phases are in equilibrium. Below the triple-point pressure a substance cannot exist as a liquid, so it sublimes; freeze-drying and dry ice depend on this.

concepts.name: The slope of the solid-liquid curve
concepts.statement: For most substances the solid-liquid curve has a positive slope, so the melting point rises with pressure; for water it has a slight negative slope, so pressure lowers the melting point of ice.

concepts.name: The critical point and supercritical fluids
concepts.statement: The liquid-gas curve ends at the critical point; above the critical temperature a gas cannot be liquefied however much pressure is applied, and the substance is a supercritical fluid whose properties are intermediate between those of a liquid and a gas.

concepts.name: Critical point
concepts.statement: The critical point of a substance is the temperature and pressure above which its gas cannot be condensed into a liquid, the point at which its liquid-gas curve ends.

concepts.name: Supercritical fluid
concepts.statement: A supercritical fluid is a substance at a temperature and pressure higher than its critical point, with properties between those of a gas and a liquid.

concepts.name: Crystalline and amorphous solids
concepts.statement: In a crystalline solid the particles are arranged in a definite repeating pattern, so every particle is held with the same forces and the solid melts at a precise temperature; in an amorphous solid they are arranged randomly, the attractions vary, and the solid softens over a range of temperatures.

concepts.name: Ionic, metallic, covalent network, and molecular solids
concepts.statement: Crystalline solids are classified by the forces between their particles, and these forces explain their properties: ionic solids are hard, brittle and conduct only when molten; metallic solids are malleable conductors; covalent network solids are very hard with very high melting points; molecular solids are soft with low melting points.

concepts.name: Classifying a crystalline solid
concepts.statement: From a formula we identify the particles (ions, metal atoms, network-forming atoms or molecules) and so the type of solid; from observed properties such as hardness, conductivity and melting point we reason back to the type.

concepts.name: Crystal defects
concepts.statement: The repeating pattern of a crystal may contain defects: vacancies where a particle is missing, particles in interstitial sites, and impurities substituted into the lattice. Defects change physical properties, and doping silicon creates them on purpose for semiconductors.

concepts.name: Crystalline solid
concepts.statement: A crystalline solid is a solid in which the particles are arranged in a definite repeating pattern.

concepts.name: Amorphous solid
concepts.statement: An amorphous solid, or noncrystalline solid, is a solid in which the particles lack an ordered internal structure.

concepts.name: Ionic solid
concepts.statement: An ionic solid is a crystalline solid composed of positive and negative ions held together by strong electrostatic attractions.

concepts.name: Metallic solid
concepts.statement: A metallic solid is a crystalline solid composed of metal atoms.

concepts.name: Covalent network solid
concepts.statement: A covalent network solid is a crystalline solid whose particles are held together by covalent bonds.

concepts.name: Molecular solid
concepts.statement: A molecular solid is a crystalline solid composed of neutral molecules held together by intermolecular forces of attraction.

concepts.name: Vacancy
concepts.statement: A vacancy is a defect in a crystal where a position that should contain an atom or ion is empty.

concepts.name: Interstitial sites
concepts.statement: Interstitial sites are the spaces between the regular particle positions in an array of atoms or ions.

concepts.name: The unit cell and the lattice systems
concepts.statement: The structure of a crystal is described by its unit cell, its simplest repeating unit, whose lattice points mark the locations of atoms or ions and which repeats in three dimensions. A unit cell is defined by three edge lengths and three angles, giving seven lattice systems and fourteen unit cells.

concepts.name: Simple, body-centered, and face-centered cubic unit cells
concepts.statement: Counting one-eighth of each corner atom, one-half of each face atom and all of a body-center atom, a simple cubic cell contains one atom, a body-centered cubic cell two and a face-centered cubic cell four. Their coordination numbers are 6, 8 and 12, and they fill about 52%, 68% and 74% of the space.

concepts.name: Hexagonal and cubic closest packing
concepts.statement: Identical spheres pack most closely in hexagonal layers, each layer sitting in the hollows of the one below. Stacking ABAB… gives hexagonal closest packing and ABCABC… gives cubic closest packing, which is the face-centered cubic structure; both have a coordination number of 12, and about two-thirds of metals crystallize this way.

concepts.name: Calculating a radius and a density from a unit cell
concepts.statement: Where the atoms touch (along an edge in a simple cubic cell, along a face diagonal in a face-centered cubic cell, along a body diagonal in a body-centered one) the edge length gives the radius; the atoms per cell times the mass of an atom, divided by the cell’s volume, gives the density. The same geometry gives ionic radii from the edge length of an ionic crystal.

concepts.name: Tetrahedral, octahedral, and cubic holes
concepts.statement: In simple ionic structures the larger anions usually form a closest-packed array and the smaller cations occupy the holes between them: tetrahedral holes, two per anion, for small cations; octahedral holes, one per anion, for larger ones; and cubic holes in a simple cubic array for the largest.

concepts.name: Finding a formula from the holes occupied
concepts.statement: Knowing the number of holes of each kind per anion, the fraction of them the cations occupy gives the ratio of cations to anions, and so the formula of the compound.

concepts.name: Unit cells of ionic compounds
concepts.statement: Ionic compounds with ions of similar size in a 1:1 ratio, such as CsCl, form a simple cubic structure; those whose ions differ more in size, such as NaCl and ZnS, form a face-centered cubic cell with the cations in octahedral or tetrahedral holes; CaF₂ is face-centered cubic with fluoride ions in all the tetrahedral holes. The contents of the cell give the formula.

concepts.name: X-ray diffraction and the Bragg equation, $n\lambda = 2d\sin\theta$
concepts.statement: X-rays scattered by atoms in adjacent crystal planes interfere constructively only when the extra distance traveled is a whole number of wavelengths, which happens at the angle given by the Bragg equation; measuring the diffraction angles gives the spacing of the planes.

forms.condition: constructive interference of X-rays scattered by planes a distance d apart

concepts.name: Space lattice
concepts.statement: The space lattice of a crystal is the set of all points within it that have identical environments.

concepts.name: Coordination number
concepts.statement: The coordination number of an atom in a crystal is the number of atoms closest to it; in a complex, it is the number of atoms bonded to the central metal atom.

concepts.name: Simple cubic unit cell
concepts.statement: A simple cubic unit cell, or primitive cubic unit cell, is a cube with lattice points only at its corners, the unit cell of the simple cubic structure.

concepts.name: Simple cubic structure
concepts.statement: The simple cubic structure is a crystalline structure whose cubic unit cell has lattice points only at the corners.

concepts.name: Body-centered cubic unit cell
concepts.statement: A body-centered cubic unit cell is the simplest repeating unit of a body-centered cubic crystal, a cube with lattice points at each corner and at its center.

concepts.name: Body-centered cubic (BCC) solid
concepts.statement: A body-centered cubic solid is a crystalline structure whose cubic unit cell has lattice points at the corners and in the center of the cell.

concepts.name: Face-centered cubic unit cell
concepts.statement: A face-centered cubic unit cell is the simplest repeating unit of a face-centered cubic crystal, a cube with lattice points at each corner and at the center of each face.

concepts.name: Face-centered cubic (FCC) solid
concepts.statement: A face-centered cubic solid is a crystalline structure whose cubic unit cell has lattice points on the corners and in the center of each face.

concepts.name: Isomorphous
concepts.statement: Substances are isomorphous when they possess the same crystalline structure.

concepts.name: Hexagonal closest packing (HCP)
concepts.statement: Hexagonal closest packing is a crystalline structure in which closely packed layers of atoms or ions are stacked in two alternating layers, ABAB….

concepts.name: Cubic closest packing (CCP)
concepts.statement: Cubic closest packing is a crystalline structure in which closely packed layers of atoms or ions are stacked in three alternating layers, ABCABC…; its unit cell is face-centered cubic.

concepts.name: Hole
concepts.statement: A hole, or interstice, is a space between the atoms or ions of a crystal.

concepts.name: Tetrahedral hole
concepts.statement: A tetrahedral hole is the space formed by four atoms or ions of a crystal at the corners of a tetrahedron.

concepts.name: Octahedral hole
concepts.statement: An octahedral hole is the open space in a crystal at the center of six particles located at the corners of an octahedron.

concepts.name: Diffraction
concepts.statement: Diffraction is the redirection of electromagnetic radiation when it encounters a physical barrier of dimensions similar to its wavelength.

concepts.name: X-ray crystallography
concepts.statement: X-ray crystallography is the experimental technique that finds the distances between the atoms of a crystal by measuring the angles at which X-rays are diffracted as they pass through it.
